pairs.title: Cafe fridge unplugged overnight
pairs.version_a: Leo closes a small café at 10 p.m. each night. One night his electric scooter's battery is almost flat, so he unplugs the café's fridge, plugs his scooter charger into its socket, and walks home, leaving the scooter to charge. He knows the café's rule that the fridge must never be unplugged, but he assumes the food will stay cold enough until he plugs the fridge back in at 7 a.m. It does not. By morning the fridge is warm, and the café has to throw away $900 worth of milk, cream and cakes. Later, the owner checks with the power company. It reports that the street had normal power from 10 p.m. until 8 a.m., so if Leo had left the fridge plugged in, the food would have stayed cold.
pairs.version_b: Leo closes a small café at 10 p.m. each night. One night his electric scooter's battery is almost flat, so he unplugs the café's fridge, plugs his scooter charger into its socket, and walks home, leaving the scooter to charge. He knows the café's rule that the fridge must never be unplugged, but he assumes the food will stay cold enough until he plugs the fridge back in at 7 a.m. It does not. By morning the fridge is warm, and the café has to throw away $900 worth of milk, cream and cakes. Later, the owner checks with the power company. It reports that a fault cut the street's power from 10 p.m. until 8 a.m., so even if Leo had left the fridge plugged in, the food would have spoiled.
pairs.intended_difference: In A the street had normal power all night, so the food would have stayed cold had Leo not unplugged the fridge; in B a power cut over the same hours means the food would have spoiled anyway.
pairs.judgment_question: How much of the $900 cost of the thrown-away food should Leo have to pay?
pairs.comprehension_question: According to the power company, what was the street's power like that night?
pairs.option_b: Cut by a fault from 10 p.m. until 8 a.m.
pairs.option_c: Cut by a fault for ten minutes around midnight
pairs.prediction_rationale: Whether someone should pay for a loss tracks closely whether the loss would have happened without them, so readers told the power cut would have spoiled the food anyway should cut Leo's share sharply, while still charging him something for breaking the rule.
pairs.originality_note: An invented workplace case about an unplugged fridge and an unknown street power cut, not based on any published vignette.

pairs.title: Shopping stop on the way to the airport
pairs.version_a: Petra offers to drive her brother Sam to the airport for a noon flight to their grandmother's 90th birthday party in another country. On the way, she insists on stopping at a shopping mall to buy a dress, although Sam warns her it could make him miss the flight. She knows he is right, but she wants the dress before the sale ends. She shops for an hour. They reach the airport after the gate has closed, and Sam misses the flight. There is no other flight until the next day, so he misses the party. That evening, Sam checks the airline's website. It shows that the flight took off on time and landed as planned, so if Petra had not stopped, Sam would have reached the party.
pairs.version_b: Petra offers to drive her brother Sam to the airport for a noon flight to their grandmother's 90th birthday party in another country. On the way, she insists on stopping at a shopping mall to buy a dress, although Sam warns her it could make him miss the flight. She knows he is right, but she wants the dress before the sale ends. She shops for an hour. They reach the airport after the gate has closed, and Sam misses the flight. There is no other flight until the next day, so he misses the party. That evening, Sam checks the airline's website. It shows that an engine fault grounded the flight until the next day, so even if Petra had not stopped, Sam would have missed the party.
pairs.intended_difference: In A the flight left and arrived as planned, so Sam would have reached the party without Petra's stop; in B an engine fault grounded the flight, so he would have missed the party anyway.
pairs.judgment_question: How much is Petra to blame for Sam missing his grandmother's birthday party?
pairs.comprehension_question: What does the airline's website show about Sam's noon flight?
pairs.option_a: It took off on time and landed as planned
pairs.option_b: An engine fault grounded it until the next day
pairs.option_c: It took off two hours late
pairs.prediction_rationale: Petra's selfish choice is the same in both versions, but the harm asked about is missing the party, and readers who learn it would have been missed anyway should give her much less blame for that particular loss.
pairs.originality_note: An original everyday family case about a missed flight and a missed party; it does not reuse any known missed-flight or regret vignette, which concern timing rather than whether the loss would have happened anyway.

pairs.title: Museum blinds and gallery heating
pairs.version_a: In an art museum, the blinds in Gallery 4 must stay down every afternoon. This is a museum rule, because when afternoon sun falls on the gallery's oldest painting while the heating is on, its paint dries out and cracks. Ben was a guard in his first week at the museum. Ben knew about this rule. At 1:30 one afternoon, Ben raised the blinds in Gallery 4 to read a newspaper by daylight, and left them up. At 2:00, Ines, the building engineer, switched on the gallery heating, as her job requires every afternoon at that time. The sun and the heat together dried out the old painting, and its paint cracked in several places. Repairs will cost $20,000. If the blinds had been down, or if the heating had not been on, the painting would not have cracked.
pairs.version_b: In an art museum, the blinds in Gallery 4 must stay down every afternoon. This is a museum rule, because when afternoon sun falls on the gallery's oldest painting while the heating is on, its paint dries out and cracks. Ben was a guard in his first week at the museum. Ben did not know about this rule. At 1:30 one afternoon, Ben raised the blinds in Gallery 4 to read a newspaper by daylight, and left them up. At 2:00, Ines, the building engineer, switched on the gallery heating, as her job requires every afternoon at that time. The sun and the heat together dried out the old painting, and its paint cracked in several places. Repairs will cost $20,000. If the blinds had been down, or if the heating had not been on, the painting would not have cracked.
pairs.intended_difference: In A Ben knew about the rule that the blinds must stay down; in B he did not know about it.
pairs.judgment_question: To what extent did Ben cause the painting to crack?
pairs.comprehension_question: Did Ben know about the museum's rule on the Gallery 4 blinds?
pairs.option_b: No, he did not know about it
pairs.prediction_rationale: Readers usually pick out a knowing rule-breaker as more of a cause than an unknowing one even when the physical contribution is the same, but some readers will hold that knowledge does not change what physically happened, which should keep the gap modest.
pairs.originality_note: An invented museum case in which sunlight and scheduled heating together damage a painting; it is not a re-skin of the pen, computer-crash or other published joint-cause vignettes.

pairs.title: Grapefruit juice on a hospital ward
pairs.version_a: On a hospital ward, patients who take the heart medicine Cardolin must never be served grapefruit juice. This is a ward rule, because Cardolin taken with grapefruit juice makes people dizzy. Nadia was a kitchen assistant in her first week on the ward. Nadia knew about this rule. At 8:30 one morning, Nadia served grapefruit juice with breakfast to Mr. Hale, a patient who takes Cardolin, because the orange juice had run out. At 9:00, Nurse Okafor gave Mr. Hale his Cardolin, as his doctor's orders require every morning at that time. Soon afterwards, Mr. Hale became dizzy, fell while walking to the bathroom, and broke his hip. If he had not had the grapefruit juice, or if he had not had the Cardolin, he would not have become dizzy.
pairs.version_b: On a hospital ward, patients who take the heart medicine Cardolin must never be served grapefruit juice. This is a ward rule, because Cardolin taken with grapefruit juice makes people dizzy. Nadia was a kitchen assistant in her first week on the ward. Nadia did not know about this rule. At 8:30 one morning, Nadia served grapefruit juice with breakfast to Mr. Hale, a patient who takes Cardolin, because the orange juice had run out. At 9:00, Nurse Okafor gave Mr. Hale his Cardolin, as his doctor's orders require every morning at that time. Soon afterwards, Mr. Hale became dizzy, fell while walking to the bathroom, and broke his hip. If he had not had the grapefruit juice, or if he had not had the Cardolin, he would not have become dizzy.
pairs.intended_difference: In A Nadia knew about the rule against serving grapefruit juice to Cardolin patients; in B she did not know about it.
pairs.judgment_question: To what extent did Nadia cause Mr. Hale's fall?
pairs.comprehension_question: Did Nadia know about the ward's rule on grapefruit juice?
pairs.option_b: No, she did not know about it
pairs.prediction_rationale: A worker who knowingly serves the forbidden drink should be seen as more of a cause of the fall than one who acted in innocent ignorance, but because the drink plays the same physical role in both versions, many readers will rate her as a real cause either way.
pairs.originality_note: An original hospital case in which a forbidden drink and a routine medicine dose together cause a fall; it does not adapt any published causal-judgment vignette.

pairs.title: Wading a flooded stream
pairs.version_a: Hugo is a hiking guide leading six adults on a paid mountain walk. Late in the afternoon, they reach a stream swollen by heavy rain. The nearest bridge is ninety minutes' walk upstream. Hugo's company advises guides not to wade across streams this high, and Hugo knows that logs carried by fast water can knock people over. But the group is tired and he wants to finish before dark, so he has the group link arms and leads them across on foot. While they cross, a log carried down by the current strikes one hiker, Mei. She is swept against the rocks and breaks her leg.
pairs.version_b: Hugo is a hiking guide leading six adults on a paid mountain walk. Late in the afternoon, they reach a stream swollen by heavy rain. The nearest bridge is ninety minutes' walk upstream. Hugo's company advises guides not to wade across streams this high, and Hugo knows that logs carried by fast water can knock people over. But the group is tired and he wants to finish before dark, so he has the group link arms and leads them across on foot. While they cross, no log comes down the current. Everyone reaches the far bank safely, and nobody is hurt in any way.
pairs.intended_difference: In A a log happens to come down the current and breaks a hiker's leg; in B no log comes down and nobody is hurt.
pairs.judgment_question: How wrong was Hugo's choice to lead the group across the stream on foot?
pairs.comprehension_question: What happened while the group was crossing the stream?
pairs.option_a: A log struck a hiker, and she broke her leg
pairs.option_b: Everyone crossed safely and nobody was hurt
pairs.option_c: Hugo slipped and lost the group's map
pairs.prediction_rationale: Readers tend to let a bad outcome color how risky and wrong a choice looks, so the injury version should be rated more wrong, but questions about the wrongness of the choice itself respond less to outcome than blame does.
pairs.originality_note: An invented outdoor case about a guide wading a flooded stream, unlike the drunk-driving and other standard moral-luck vignettes.

pairs.title: Client file over cafe Wi-Fi
pairs.version_a: Farah is an accountant. While waiting at an airport café, she gets an urgent request from a client, Mr. Ortiz, for a copy of his tax file, which includes his bank details and ID number. Her firm's rules say client files must be sent only over a secure connection, because thieves sometimes spy on public Wi-Fi. Farah knows this, but her secure connection is not working, and she does not want to keep Mr. Ortiz waiting until her flight lands, so she sends the file over the café's free Wi-Fi. As it happens, a thief in the café is spying on that network. He copies the file and takes out $8,000 of loans in Mr. Ortiz's name, which take months to sort out.
pairs.version_b: Farah is an accountant. While waiting at an airport café, she gets an urgent request from a client, Mr. Ortiz, for a copy of his tax file, which includes his bank details and ID number. Her firm's rules say client files must be sent only over a secure connection, because thieves sometimes spy on public Wi-Fi. Farah knows this, but her secure connection is not working, and she does not want to keep Mr. Ortiz waiting until her flight lands, so she sends the file over the café's free Wi-Fi. As it happens, nobody in the café is spying on that network. The file reaches Mr. Ortiz safely, no one else ever sees his details, and nothing bad comes of it.
pairs.intended_difference: In A a thief who happens to be on the café network steals the file and misuses the client's details; in B nobody is spying and the file arrives safely.
pairs.judgment_question: How wrong was Farah's choice to send the file over the café's free Wi-Fi?
pairs.comprehension_question: What happened after Farah sent the file?
pairs.option_a: A thief in the café copied it and took out loans in Mr. Ortiz's name
pairs.option_b: It reached Mr. Ortiz safely and nobody else saw it
pairs.option_c: It never arrived, so she sent it again after landing
pairs.prediction_rationale: The stolen-identity outcome should make the same rule-breaking choice look more reckless and wrong, but the choice already looks somewhat wrong when nothing happens, so the gap should be moderate rather than large.
pairs.originality_note: An original case about a data-security risk and financial harm, with no counterpart among famous thought experiments or published moral-luck vignettes.
